```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(ggplot2)
```

fMRI noise is autocorrelated: what the scanner records at one volume
predicts part of what it records at the next. Ordinary least squares (OLS)
ignores this. Its coefficient estimates remain unbiased, but its standard
errors come out too small, so its *t* statistics are too large and a 5%
threshold lets through more than 5% of voxels that have no real effect.

Prewhitening fixes this. You estimate the noise's autocorrelation from the
residuals of a first OLS fit, build the filter that turns that noise back into
independent values, apply the same filter to the data and to the design
matrix, and fit again. fmriAR does the estimation and the filtering. This
vignette walks through the four steps on simulated data where the truth is
known, so each step can be checked.

## A simulated study

Two five-minute runs at a repetition time (TR) of 2 seconds. The task is a
series of brief events, 12 to 20 seconds apart, convolved with a canonical
haemodynamic response. The design also has an intercept for each run and three
slow cosine drift terms per run, as most fMRI models do.

```{r design}
library(fmriAR)
set.seed(2024)

TR <- 2
n_per_run <- 150
runs <- rep(1:2, each = n_per_run)   # a run label for every volume
n_time <- length(runs)

# Brief events 12-20 s apart, convolved with a canonical HRF
hrf <- function(t) dgamma(t, 6) - dgamma(t, 16) / 6
h <- hrf(seq(0, 30, by = TR))
event_regressor <- function(n) {
  onsets <- cumsum(sample(6:10, n, replace = TRUE))
  stim <- tabulate(onsets[onsets <= n], nbins = n)
  x <- stats::filter(stim, h / max(h), sides = 1)
  as.numeric(replace(x, is.na(x), 0))
}

# Three slow cosines per run absorb scanner drift
cosines <- function(n, k) {
  sapply(seq_len(k), function(j) cos(pi * j * (seq_len(n) - 0.5) / n))
}
none <- matrix(0, n_per_run, 3)

X <- cbind(c(event_regressor(n_per_run), event_regressor(n_per_run)),
           runs == 1, runs == 2,
           rbind(cosines(n_per_run, 3), none),
           rbind(none, cosines(n_per_run, 3)))
colnames(X) <- c("task", "run1", "run2", paste0("drift", 1:6))
```

The noise in each voxel is a first-order autoregressive process, AR(1), with
coefficient 0.5: each volume's noise is half the previous volume's plus a fresh
random shock. Each run is simulated separately, as two scanning sessions would
be. One voxel in ten responds to the task; the rest have no effect at all,
which is what lets us count false positives.

```{r data}
n_vox <- 10000
active <- 1:1000
null <- setdiff(seq_len(n_vox), active)

ar1_run <- function() as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.5), n = n_per_run))
noise <- replicate(n_vox, c(ar1_run(), ar1_run()))

beta <- ifelse(seq_len(n_vox) %in% active, 0.5, 0)
Y <- noise + outer(X[, "task"], beta)
```

## The problem: OLS on autocorrelated noise

Fit OLS to every voxel and compute a *t* statistic for the task.
`sandwich_from_whitened_resid()` returns ordinary OLS standard errors when it
is handed the unwhitened design and data.

```{r ols}
ols <- lm.fit(X, Y)
se_ols <- sandwich_from_whitened_resid(X, Y, beta = ols$coefficients)$se
t_ols <- ols$coefficients["task", ] / se_ols[1, ]

# Share of no-effect voxels that pass |t| > 1.96
mean(abs(t_ols[null]) > 1.96)
```

```{r fpr-ols, include = FALSE}
fpr_ols <- mean(abs(t_ols[null]) > 1.96)
```

The threshold promises 5%. OLS delivers `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * fpr_ols)`.

## Step 1: Estimate the noise model

`fit_noise()` estimates the autocorrelation from the OLS residuals and fits an
autoregressive model to it. By default it chooses the order by BIC
(`p = "auto"`) and pools all voxels and runs into one model
(`pooling = "global"`). Lag products never span the boundary between runs.

```{r fit}
plan <- fit_noise(ols$residuals, runs = runs, design = X)
plan
```

The search chose an AR(1) and estimated its coefficient at
`r sprintf("%.2f", plan$phi[[1]][1])`; the truth is 0.5.

Pass `design = X` whenever the residuals come from a fitted model. Removing
the fitted model also removes some of the noise's autocorrelation, so
residuals look less autocorrelated than the noise really is. The larger the
design, the stronger the pull, and drift terms pull hardest. `design = X`
corrects for it. Without the correction, fits that pool thousands of voxels
can also pick an AR order that is too high. *Refining the noise model*
(`vignette("fmriAR-noise-models")`) shows both effects.

## Step 2: Whiten the design and the data

`whiten_apply()` runs the filter over every column of `X` and `Y`, restarting
it at the beginning of each run. Your inputs are not modified.

```{r whiten}
w <- whiten_apply(plan, X, Y, runs = runs)
```

For an AR(1) the filter is one subtraction: each whitened value is the
original value minus `r sprintf("%.2f", plan$phi[[1]][1])` times the value one
volume earlier. That removes the part of the noise the previous volume
predicts and leaves the fresh shock. The first volume of each run has no
predecessor, so it is rescaled instead, by $\sqrt{1 - \phi^2}$, which makes
the result exact generalised least squares (GLS).

The same filter must be applied to the design. The model says data = design
× coefficients + noise. Filtering both sides with the same filter keeps that
equation intact and leaves only the noise whitened.

```{r fig-filter, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 2.9, fig.cap = "The task regressor before (grey) and after (blue) whitening, volumes 40 to 100 of run 1. Each blue value is the grey value minus half the grey value one volume earlier. Every voxel's data passes through the same filter."}
win <- 40:100
fd <- data.frame(t = win, before = X[win, "task"], after = w$X[win, "task"])
pk <- win[which.max(fd$before)]                 # label beside the tallest peak
ggplot(fd, aes(t)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey75") +
  geom_line(aes(y = before), colour = "grey65", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = after, colour = "Whitened"), linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = pk + 1.3, y = fd$before[fd$t == pk], label = "before",
           hjust = 0, size = 3.1, colour = "grey45") +
  annotate("text", x = pk - 1.5, y = fd$after[fd$t == pk - 1],
           label = "whitened", hjust = 1, size = 3.1) +
  albersdown::scale_color_albers(limits = c("Whitened", "OLS"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Volume (TR = 2 s)", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

The whitened regressor rises earlier and falls faster than the original,
and dips below zero after each response. Whitening keeps the changes in a
signal and discounts its slow, sustained parts, because slow drifts are
exactly what autocorrelated noise produces on its own.

## Step 3: Refit and compute standard errors

Fit the whitened data on the whitened design. With white noise, the ordinary
formula for standard errors is the right one.

```{r refit}
gls <- lm.fit(w$X, w$Y)
se_gls <- sandwich_from_whitened_resid(w$X, w$Y, beta = gls$coefficients)$se
t_gls <- gls$coefficients["task", ] / se_gls[1, ]
```

Because the simulation tells us which voxels have an effect, we can check
each fit against the truth. Over the 9,000 voxels with no effect, the
*reported* standard error should match the *actual* spread of the estimates,
and 5% of those voxels should pass the threshold.

```{r compare}
summarise_fit <- function(b, se) {
  c(`reported SE`    = mean(se[1, null]),
    `actual SD`      = sd(b["task", null]),
    `false positive` = mean(abs(b["task", null] / se[1, null]) > 1.96),
    `true positive`  = mean(abs(b["task", active] / se[1, active]) > 1.96))
}
knitr::kable(
  rbind(OLS = summarise_fit(ols$coefficients, se_ols),
        prewhitened = summarise_fit(gls$coefficients, se_gls)),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Task effect, OLS against prewhitened GLS, scored against the simulation's truth."
)
```

The excess grows as the threshold tightens, which is where whole-brain
analyses operate:

```{r alpha-table}
rejection_rate <- function(t, alpha) mean(abs(t[null]) > qnorm(1 - alpha / 2))
alpha <- c(0.05, 0.01, 0.001)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * x)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(threshold = pct(alpha),
             OLS = pct(sapply(alpha, rejection_rate, t = t_ols)),
             prewhitened = pct(sapply(alpha, rejection_rate, t = t_gls))),
  align = "rrr",
  caption = "Share of no-effect voxels declared significant at each threshold."
)
```

OLS reports a standard error smaller than its estimates' real spread, and its
false-positive rate more than doubles. After prewhitening the two agree and
the rate is back near 5%. The estimates themselves are also less variable, so
little real sensitivity is lost: much of OLS's higher hit rate came from the
same too-small standard error that produced its false positives.

```{r fig-null, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.6, fig.cap = "The task t statistic in the 9,000 voxels with no effect. The curve is the standard normal distribution a valid test assumes. Orange bars, beyond ±1.96, are false positives."}
n_null <- length(null)
fpr <- c(mean(abs(t_ols[null]) > 1.96), mean(abs(t_gls[null]) > 1.96))
lev <- c(sprintf("OLS: %.1f%% of null voxels pass |t| > 1.96", 100 * fpr[1]),
         sprintf("Whitened: %.1f%% (a valid test gives 5%%)", 100 * fpr[2]))
tn <- data.frame(fit = factor(rep(lev, each = n_null), levels = lev),
                 t = c(t_ols[null], t_gls[null]))
tn$tail <- ifelse(abs(tn$t) > 1.96, "false positive", "inside")
bw <- 1.96 / 7                    # a bin edge sits exactly on the threshold
curve <- data.frame(t = seq(-5, 5, by = 0.02))
curve$d <- dnorm(curve$t)
curve_lab <- data.frame(fit = factor(lev[1], levels = lev), t = 1.15, d = 0.36,
                        txt = "standard normal:\nwhat a valid test gives")
ggplot(tn, aes(t)) +
  geom_histogram(data = subset(tn, tail == "inside"),
                 aes(y = after_stat(count / (n_null * bw))),
                 binwidth = bw, boundary = 0, fill = "grey78") +
  geom_histogram(data = subset(tn, tail == "false positive"),
                 aes(y = after_stat(count / (n_null * bw)), fill = "OLS"),
                 binwidth = bw, boundary = 0) +
  geom_line(data = curve, aes(t, d), colour = "grey25", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(data = curve_lab, aes(t, d, label = txt), hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
            size = 3.1, lineheight = 0.95, colour = "grey25") +
  facet_wrap(~fit, ncol = 1) +
  albersdown::scale_fill_albers(limits = c("Whitened", "OLS"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-1.96, 0, 1.96), labels = c("-1.96", "0", "1.96")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-5, 5), ylim = c(0, 0.45)) +
  labs(x = "t statistic, no-effect voxels", y = NULL) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0),
        panel.grid.major = element_blank())
```

## Step 4: Check that whitening worked

If the filter matches the noise, what is left over should be white: a
voxel's residual at one volume should say nothing about the next.
`acorr_diagnostics()` measures each voxel's autocorrelation at lags 1, 2, …,
centring each run separately and never pairing volumes across a run boundary.

```{r acf}
resid_w <- w$Y - w$X %*% gls$coefficients
ac_before <- acorr_diagnostics(ols$residuals, runs = runs, max_lag = 10,
                               aggregate = "none")
ac_after <- acorr_diagnostics(resid_w, runs = runs, max_lag = 10,
                              aggregate = "none")

# Share of voxels whose lag-1 autocorrelation falls outside the
# 95% range expected of white noise
c(before = mean(abs(ac_before$acf[1, ]) > ac_before$ci),
  after  = mean(abs(ac_after$acf[1, ]) > ac_after$ci))
```

`ci` is $1.96 / \sqrt{n}$: 95% of a white-noise series' autocorrelations
fall within $\pm$`ci`. It describes one voxel, so compare it with the spread
across voxels, not with their average, which varies far less. Before
whitening, every voxel's lag-1 autocorrelation lies outside the range. After,
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(abs(ac_after$acf[1, ]) > ac_after$ci))` do,
close to the 5% expected of white noise.

```{r fig-acf, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Each voxel's autocorrelation at lags 1 to 10. Lines span the middle 95% of the 10,000 voxels; dots mark the median. The grey band is where 95% of one voxel's values fall if its noise is white."}
acf_summary <- function(a, stage) {
  data.frame(stage = stage, lag = a$lags,
             lo = apply(a$acf, 1, quantile, 0.025),
             mid = apply(a$acf, 1, median),
             hi = apply(a$acf, 1, quantile, 0.975))
}
lev <- c("OLS", "Whitened")
acs <- rbind(acf_summary(ac_before, lev[1]), acf_summary(ac_after, lev[2]))
acs$stage <- factor(acs$stage, levels = lev)
ci <- ac_after$ci
band_lab <- data.frame(stage = factor(lev[2], levels = lev), lag = 10.4, y = ci,
                       txt = "white-noise range")
ggplot(acs, aes(lag)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -ci, ymax = ci,
           fill = "grey88") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, colour = stage), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = mid, colour = stage), size = 1.8) +
  geom_text(data = band_lab, aes(lag, y, label = txt), hjust = 1, vjust = -0.5,
            size = 3, colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~stage) +
  albersdown::scale_color_albers(limits = c("Whitened", "OLS"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 5, 10)) +
  labs(x = "Lag (volumes)", y = "Autocorrelation") +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

The whitened values centre slightly below zero, at about
`r sprintf("%.2f", median(ac_after$acf))`. That is expected: fitting a model
makes its residuals slightly negatively autocorrelated, and the more
regressors per run, the larger the shift. It is also why the share outside
the band is a little above 5%.

If some autocorrelation remains, for example because the model order was too
low, `sandwich_from_whitened_resid(..., type = "hac", runs = runs)` gives
standard errors that tolerate it (Newey–West, within runs).

## Common situations

### Several runs

`pooling = "global"` (the default) fits one noise model to all runs. Use
`pooling = "run"` to give each run its own coefficients, for instance when
runs differ in length or acquisition.

```{r pooling-run}
plan_by_run <- fit_noise(ols$residuals, runs = runs, design = X,
                         pooling = "run")
plan_by_run$phi
```

### Scrubbed frames

Frames flagged for motion are passed as `censor`, as indices or as a
logical vector with one entry per volume. They are left out of the noise
estimate, and the filter restarts after each one so that no flagged value
leaks into its neighbours. The whitened output keeps every row and lists the
censored ones in `censor`; drop them before fitting.

```{r censor}
scrub <- c(50:52, 170)
plan_c <- fit_noise(ols$residuals, runs = runs, design = X, censor = scrub)
w_c <- whiten_apply(plan_c, X, Y, runs = runs)

keep <- setdiff(seq_len(n_time), w_c$censor)
fit_c <- lm.fit(w_c$X[keep, ], w_c$Y[keep, ])
```

`whiten_apply()` reuses the plan's censor set when the data have the length
the plan was fitted on, as here; pass `censor` yourself otherwise.

### One call

`whiten()` fits the OLS model, estimates the plan and whitens in one step.
Arguments after `censor` go to `fit_noise()`.

```{r one-call}
w1 <- whiten(X, Y, runs = runs, design = X)
```

### Large data

Whitening runs in parallel over voxels when fmriAR was built with OpenMP.
`options(fmriAR.max_threads = k)` caps the number of threads.
